Lighthouse keeping

By Ada Quill

Lighthouse keeping is the work of tending a lighthouse: keeping the lamp lit through the night, the lens clean, and the clockwork that turned the light wound on schedule. For most of the history of coastal navigation it was a resident trade, carried on by families who lived at the station for years at a time, often far from the nearest town, with supplies brought by boat when the weather allowed.

The work was repetitive and exacting. A light that went dark for even part of a night could cost a ship, and keepers were expected to log every watch, every change in the weather, and every vessel that passed. Their logbooks survive in many archives and are now read by historians of shipping, of climate, and of the families themselves.

History

[edit]

The earliest lights were open fires on headlands, tended by watchmen who carried wood or coal up to the platform by hand. As towers grew taller and lamps more elaborate, the job became a profession with its own rules, uniforms, and inspections. Keepers were paid by harbour authorities or by the crown, and the post often passed from parent to child along with the knowledge of the particular coast.

By the nineteenth century most maritime nations ran a lighthouse service with written standing orders. Those orders told the keeper when to light the lamp, how to trim the wick, how to polish the brass, and what to do when the fog came in and the bell or the horn had to be sounded at fixed intervals until morning.

Early lights

[edit]

Before the invention of the lens, a light was only as good as its fuel and the care with which it was tended. Coal fires smoked and dimmed in wet weather; candles guttered in drafts. Keepers learned to read the wind and to bank the fire against it, and a good keeper was one whose light could be seen from the same distance every night of the year.

The arrival of oil lamps with reflectors changed the work from stoking to cleaning. Soot was now the enemy, and the daily round began with trimming wicks and polishing the silvered reflectors until the next lighting time came around again at dusk.

Duties¶

A keeper's day was built around the light. In the morning the lens was cleaned and covered against the sun, which could otherwise focus through the glass and start a fire. In the afternoon the lamp was filled and the wick trimmed. At sunset the light was lit, and through the night the keeper stood watches, winding the clockwork that turned the lens and checking the flame at set intervals.

Beyond the light itself there was the station to keep: paint to renew against the salt, the fog signal to maintain, stores to count, and the logbook to fill in with a clear hand. Inspectors arrived without warning and judged a station as much by its brasswork as by its light.

The night watch

The night was divided into watches shared between the keepers of a station. The keeper on watch climbed the tower at fixed times to check the flame and wind the clockwork, and recorded the visibility, the wind, and any ships seen. On a single-keeper station the whole night fell to one person, and sleep came in short pieces between the rounds.

Storms made the watch dangerous as well as long. Spray could reach the lantern room on exposed rocks, and keepers wrote of nights spent wiping the glass from inside while the tower shook with each wave that broke against its base.
